options.content: A new, inventive and useful invention
options.rationale: Correct: patents protect how an invention works.

options.content: The name and logo of a business
options.rationale: That is a trademark.

options.content: The text of a novel or a song's lyrics
options.rationale: That is copyright.

options.content: The colour scheme of a website
options.rationale: This is not what patents protect.

explanation: A patent gives the inventor exclusive rights to a new invention for a limited period.

stem: Which intellectual property right protects an app's **name and logo**?

options.rationale: Correct: trademarks protect brand names, logos and slogans.
Patents protect inventions.
Industrial designs protect a product's shape or pattern.
Trade secrets are confidential information, not public brands.

explanation: Names and logos that identify a business's goods or services are trademarks.

stem: The source code of a newly written program is protected by:

options.rationale: Patents are never automatic; they must be applied for.
Correct: code is an original work and copyright arises when it is created.
Trademarks protect brands, not code.
Designs protect appearance, not code.

explanation: Software code is protected by copyright as soon as it is written.

stem: Which organisation should a Zimbabwean technology business register with in order to pay income tax?

options.rationale: ZIPO registers patents, trademarks and designs.

options.content: The Postal and Telecommunications Regulatory Authority
options.rationale: POTRAZ regulates telecommunications.
Correct: ZIMRA collects taxes.
ZIMSEC runs examinations.

explanation: Businesses register with ZIMRA, declare income and pay tax.

stem: A Harare company creates a phone stand with an unusual curved shape that customers recognise. Which right protects the **shape**?

options.rationale: Copyright protects creative works such as code and text.
Correct: it protects a product's appearance.
A patent protects how something works, not its look.
The shape is visible to everyone, so it cannot be secret.

explanation: The appearance (shape, pattern, lines) of a product is protected by registering an industrial design.

stem: Why should an inventor apply for a patent **before** showing the invention at a trade fair?

options.content: Trade fairs only accept products that already have patents
options.rationale: This is not the main reason.

options.content: The patent fee doubles after any trade fair
options.rationale: Fees are not linked to trade fairs.

options.content: Copyright stops applying once a product is shown
options.rationale: Copyright is not affected; patentability is.

options.content: Public disclosure can mean the invention is no longer new
options.rationale: Correct: novelty is required for a patent.

explanation: An invention must be new to be patented; showing it publicly first can destroy its novelty.
hints: What happens to novelty when an invention is shown in public?

stem: An online shop sells its customers' phone numbers to advertisers without consent. Which law has it most likely broken?

options.content: The Copyright and Neighbouring Rights Act
options.rationale: Copyright concerns creative works.
No invention is involved.

options.content: The Cyber and Data Protection Act
options.rationale: Correct: it governs the use of personal data.
No brand is involved.

explanation: Using personal data without consent breaks data protection law: the Cyber and Data Protection Act [Chapter 12:07].

stem: A start-up's secret algorithm for detecting fraud would be easy for competitors to copy if they saw it, and it may not be patentable. What is the **best** way to protect it?

options.content: Publish it online with a copyright notice
options.rationale: Publishing reveals the idea; copyright protects only the exact code.

options.content: Register the algorithm as a trademark
options.rationale: Trademarks protect brand names and logos.

options.content: Register the algorithm as an industrial design
options.rationale: Designs protect appearance, not methods.

options.content: Keep it as a trade secret with NDAs for staff
options.rationale: Correct: confidentiality protects it without publishing how it works.

explanation: Valuable know-how that cannot or should not be published is best protected as a trade secret, backed by non-disclosure agreements.
hints: Which method needs no registration and protects confidential know-how?

stem: Copyright protects the code of a program but not the idea behind it.
explanation: True. Another programmer may write different code that achieves the same thing without infringing copyright.

stem: A patent lasts for ever once it has been granted.
explanation: False. A patent lasts for a limited period, usually 20 years, after which anyone may use the invention.

stem: Match each intellectual property right to what it protects.

right.content: The shape or pattern of a product
Original works such as code, text and images

explanation: Patent: invention. Copyright: works. Trademark: brand. Industrial design: appearance.

stem: Match each duty of a technology business to the area of law it comes from.

left.content: Declaring profits and paying income tax
Getting consent before collecting users' personal data
Describing products honestly and honouring guarantees
Paying at least the agreed minimum wage

explanation: Tax: profits. Data protection: consent. Consumer protection: honest sales. Employment: wages.
hints: Link each duty to the area of law.

payload.template: Patents and trademarks in Zimbabwe are registered with the Zimbabwe Intellectual {{blank:a}} Office. A contract in which a partner promises to keep information confidential is a non-{{blank:b}} agreement.

explanation: Zimbabwe Intellectual Property Office (ZIPO); non-disclosure agreement (NDA).
hints: Both offices have their headquarters in Harare.

stem: Name the intellectual property right that exists automatically, without registration, as soon as an original work is created.
explanation: Copyright is automatic; patents, registered trademarks and industrial designs must be applied for.

stem: Explain **three** reasons why intellectual property rights are important to a technopreneur.

points.description: Stop competitors copying the product, so the investment pays off
IP can be licensed or sold for income (royalties)
Registered IP is an asset that attracts investors / supports loans / builds brand trust

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: IPR stops competitors from copying her product, so the money she spent developing it is rewarded. She can license her patent to other manufacturers for royalties. Registered IP also makes the business more valuable to investors.

explanation: IPR protects investment, creates income and adds value to the business.
hints: Think of income, competitors and investors.

stem: Nyasha is starting an online tutoring business in Bulawayo that collects learners' names and phone numbers. Describe **four** legal requirements she must meet.

points.description: Register the business name or company (with the Registrar of Companies)
Register with ZIMRA and pay tax on profits / keep financial records
Follow the Cyber and Data Protection Act: consent, secure storage of learners' data
Use licensed software and materials (copyright) / consumer protection: honest prices and terms / employment law for tutors

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: She must register her business name, register with ZIMRA and pay tax on her profits, obtain consent from learners (or parents) and store their data securely under the Cyber and Data Protection Act, and use only licensed software and learning materials.

explanation: A technology business must meet registration, tax, data protection and other legal duties.

stem: Farai's start-up in Mutare makes *AquaAlert* (fictional), a borehole-monitoring device. It has a new type of sensor circuit, firmware he wrote, a distinctive dome-shaped casing, and the brand name AquaAlert with a blue drop logo.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Match each asset to the right that protects it.
parts.explanation: Circuit: patent. Firmware: copyright. Casing: industrial design. Name and logo: trademark.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe **two** steps Farai should take before showing *AquaAlert* to possible manufacturers.

points.description: Apply for the patent (and design/trademark) before disclosing / search existing registrations
Ask manufacturers to sign a non-disclosure agreement / keep technical details confidential

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: He should file his patent application and register the design and trademark with ZIPO before showing it, and ask each manufacturer to sign a non-disclosure agreement.

hints: Each asset has its own right.

stem: *QuickFix Phones* (fictional), a phone-repair business in Harare, has been reported for several problems: it has never registered with the tax authority; it installs pirated software on customers' phones; it advertises 'a 12-month guarantee' but refuses all repairs under guarantee; and it copies customers' contacts to sell to marketers.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Match each problem to the law broken.

left.content: Not registered with the tax authority

parts.explanation: Tax: ZIMRA. Pirated software: copyright. Broken guarantee: consumer protection. Selling contacts: data protection.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain the likely consequences for the business.

points.description: Legal: fines, back taxes and penalties, prosecution, closure
Business: loss of customers' trust / damaged reputation / lost income

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The owner could be fined, made to pay back taxes with penalties, or prosecuted, and the shop could be closed. Customers who learn of the data selling and broken guarantees would stop using it, so its income would fall.

explanation: (a) Tax, copyright, consumer protection, data protection.
hints: Name the law and the duty broken.
